Q23.human: I'm a late-stage graduate student, so my use of social media platforms is different than that of established PIs. I use Twitter and Facebook for sharing content, but also for learning about science that is OUTSIDE of my field. For example, by following the Scientific Reports twitter account, I saw an article and learned about plants responding to tactile stimuli. I'm a human physiology researcher, but the larger my breadth of knowledge, the more things I can draw upon for my future studies! These are things that I would not normally find by digging around on PubMed (which is also becoming a social site itself with comments, etc). Social media also serves to show me content that lots of people are talking about, particularly for hot topics like CRISPR. /  / In addition, I use social media for outreach. For over a year, I served as a social media manager for a fledgling public science outreach group that aimed to bring science from real scientists to middle and high school students though a variety of ways, but also to adults through science cafes. Our social media presence is why the group grew and later got absorbed by a larger outreach group, and I found that the public was actually seeking groups like us to learn from. People LIKE talking to scientists, but they don't know how to get to us, and are often intimidated because of the stigma behind being a scientist. They don't get that we're just normal people who do science. Social media is a highly effective platform to address science to the public, and it can be done in ways that are not intimidating to the public, but only if it is done correctly. That is something I'm happy to discuss if there is any way to link information. This makes social media highly important for my career as a scientist; so long as there is fear, miscommunication, and distance between scientists and the public, we're going to have a hard time moving forward. Thus, by being one of the people who tries to take science to nonscientists in a fun and inviting way, I'm helping my career and that of others... and having fun doing so!

variants.t: Science communication and public outreach are HUGE for me — I actually manage the social media presence for a public science group, so a big chunk of my time goes into translating complex research into something a general audience can genuinely engage with and get excited about. Twitter and Facebook have been invaluable for that, not just as broadcast tools but as two-way conversations where members of the public ask questions and push back in ways that honestly sharpen my own thinking about my work. I also use social media heavily to follow researchers OUTSIDE my immediate field — physiology connects to so much (nutrition, neuroscience, exercise science, medicine) and Twitter in particular lets me stay across conversations I'd never encounter in a PubMed search alone. That kind of cross-disciplinary browsing has fed directly back into my PhD more than once, which I find really useful and kind of underrated as a benefit of these platforms!

Science communication is HUGE for me — I actually manage the social media accounts for a public science group, so I use Twitter and Facebook to actively engage the general public with research findings, not just other researchers. It goes well beyond sharing papers; we're talking about creating accessible content that reaches OUTSIDE the academic bubble to people who would never stumble across a journal article on their own. There is this incredible appetite out there for science that most researchers don't even realise exists, and honestly that's what drives me to keep posting even when it feels like a lot of work on top of the PhD. I also use it for interdisciplinary learning — following researchers in completely unrelated fields has genuinely shaped how I think about my own work in human physiology. you'd be surprised how much a thread on ecology or cognitive science can spark something totally unexpected in your own research!

Science outreach, honestly — it's kind of my main thing. I manage accounts for a public science group so I use Twitter and Facebook pretty constantly to share research with non-academic audiences, not just other researchers.
Science outreach DEFINITELY -- sharing research findings with a non-specialist audience is something I do almost daily on Twitter and Facebook!

Q63.human: I desperately want to make research directly accessible and digestible by the public. I am a researcher first and foremost, but I watch my nonscientist family and friends trying to learn what I do and getting frustrated. They want to learn and know, but it is hard when you don't have 10 years of science education.

variants.t:
The single biggest thing publishers could do — and this feels almost embarrassingly obvious — is make open access the DEFAULT rather than the expensive exception. Right now when I share a paper on Twitter and someone from the general public clicks the link, they hit a paywall, and that's the moment the whole exercise collapses. You've done the hard work of translating research into something accessible and interesting, and then the publisher slams a door in their face. It undermines everything social media can do for dissemination in a really fundamental way, and I find it honestly pretty maddening.

Beyond that, I'd love to see publishers invest seriously in lay summaries — not as an afterthought, but as a genuine deliverable required at submission and written by the authors themselves rather than a PR team that doesn't understand the science. A well-written plain-language summary sitting alongside every article would give researchers who WANT to share their work something concrete and pre-approved to build from. Graphical abstracts that are actually designed to be shared on social platforms (not just squashed into a journal sidebar) would help too.

And honestly, I think publishers should be actively TRAINING researchers in science communication as part of publication support — workshops, resources, even just clear guidance on how to translate findings for a general audience. There is an enormous appetite out there for accessible science and publishers are sitting on a goldmine of content they're doing almost nothing to help researchers activate. That gap between what exists in journals and what the public can actually reach and understand feels like one of the most solvable problems in academic communication right now, if publishers were willing to treat it as their problem too.

Open access is the single biggest thing publishers could do, and I know that's not a new argument but it bears repeating because it is DIRECTLY relevant to social media usefulness — if I tweet about a paper and someone clicks through to a paywall, that conversation dies instantly. The whole point of reaching beyond the academic bubble collapses the second a curious member of the public hits a "subscribe for $35" screen. So making more content freely available, or at minimum providing a publicly accessible summary or lay abstract as standard, would transform what researchers can actually do with social media outreach. Beyond access, I'd love to see publishers invest in better sharing infrastructure — things like automatically generated tweet-length summaries, shareable visual abstracts, or even short video abstracts that researchers could post directly. Some journals are starting to do this and honestly it makes such a difference; you shouldn't need to be a graphic designer on top of everything else to communicate your work effectively online. I'd also really value some kind of altmetrics integration that's actually prominent and meaningful rather than a tiny badge buried in the sidebar — if you could see in real time that your paper had been discussed in 200 tweets or picked up by a science communicator with 50,000 followers, that would reinforce to researchers that this stuff MATTERS and encourage more of them to engage. Publishers have enormous reach and credibility, and I think they're leaving a lot on the table by not positioning themselves as active partners in public science communication rather than just gatekeepers of the final product. If they leaned into that role, it would benefit everyone — including their own visibility and relevance in a landscape that's changing really fast.

More open access would help enormously — paywalled papers are a real barrier when you're trying to share research with public audiences. Shareable summaries or even just better graphics for key findings would make a HUGE difference for outreach work honestly.

Open access, full stop — that would make EVERYTHING easier. When I share research on Twitter or Facebook, the biggest barrier is people clicking through to a paywall, and you can see the engagement just die. If publishers made it genuinely frictionless to share full-text links that actually work for non-institutional readers, I think the reach of academic research would increase dramatically. Better social sharing metadata (so previews actually look good when posted) would honestly help too -- it sounds minor but it matters when you're trying to catch someone's attention in a feed.

Social media has been genuinely transformative for how I stay current with research — and I don't say that lightly. Twitter in particular functions almost like a live-updating journal club where I can follow not just the published papers but the conversations AROUND them: the debates, the replication attempts, the methodological critiques that never make it into the paper itself. That kind of behind-the-scenes scientific discourse is incredibly valuable for a PhD student trying to understand not just what findings are emerging but how science actually works as a process. I've also found that the cross-disciplinary reach is something traditional academic resources genuinely cant match — PubMed is great for finding literature in my field, but Twitter is where I discover that a nutritional biochemist or a sleep researcher is working on something that maps perfectly onto a question I've been wrestling with. And honestly, the public engagement dimension feeds back into research support too: when I'm explaining physiology concepts to a general audience and they push back with questions I haven't considered, it sharpens my own understanding in ways that feel REAL in a way that writing for peer review alone doesn't always do.

Incredibly useful for staying current — I find out about new papers and discussions way faster through Twitter than any journal alert. The interdisciplinary stuff especially, things I'd NEVER find if I was only searching PubMed. Honestly it's transformed how I develop research ideas.

Sharing professional content through social media has genuinely changed what "dissemination" means to me — it's no longer just uploading a PDF to ResearchGate and hoping someone stumbles across it. Twitter and Facebook let you actively PUSH findings into conversations where they're relevant, and more importantly, you can share them in forms that are accessible to people who would never read the journal article itself. I think this is CRITICALLY important for publicly-funded research: if our work matters, we have an obligation to make it legible beyond the paywall and beyond the jargon. I've had moments where I share a simplified thread about a physiology concept and the response from the public is enormous — people are genuinely hungry for this kind of content, and that's not something you'd ever know if you only published through traditional venues. The challenge, honestly, is that most researchers haven't been trained to translate their work for a general audience, and social media almost forces you to develop that skill because you lose people immediately if you lean too heavily on technical language. I find that constraint incredibly useful for my own development as a scientist and communicator — it makes you interrogate what you actually understand versus what you can only describe in field-specific shorthand.

Sharing professional content is where social media REALLY shines for me, and I think it's one of the most underutilised aspects by researchers who are still stuck in the "just email a PDF" mindset. When I share a paper or a summary of a finding on Twitter, it doesn't just reach the 12 people who subscribed to that journal's alert — it reaches curious people across disciplines, students who couldn't access the paywalled version, and honestly just members of the public who are genuinely interested and never knew this research existed. The reach is incomparable to anything traditional publishing offers. Facebook has been particularly useful for sharing longer-form content through our science group page, where we can actually have a conversation with people in the comments rather than just broadcasting into a void. I do think researchers undersell themselves here — there's sometimes this attitude that dumbing down for social media compromises your work, but I'd argue the opposite: learning to explain your research clearly enough for a general audience actually deepens your own understanding of it. The sharing piece is what gets science OUT of the ivory tower, and I genuinely dont think we leverage it anywhere near as much as we could.
Twitter especially -- sharing a paper link with a good caption gets way more reach than any institutional channel, OUTSIDE academia I mean.

Really useful for sharing papers and getting them seen OUTSIDE the usual academic bubble -- I've had members of the public engage with my research in ways that just wouldn't happen through traditional channels. Twitter especially feels like it reaches people who are genuinely curious but would never stumble across a journal article on their own.

Promotion is where I think social media really separates itself from traditional academic channels in a way that's almost impossible to overstate. When I publish something — or when someone in my network does — the ability to actually DRIVE people toward that work, rather than passively hoping it gets discovered, is a fundamentally different model of academic communication. Twitter in particular lets you frame why a piece of work matters, who it's relevant to, and what question it's answering before someone even clicks the link — that context is half the battle when you're competing for attention in an information-saturated environment. I've watched relatively niche physiology papers get genuinely wide traction because someone took the time to explain in plain language why the finding was surprising or important, and that promotional effort clearly came from the researcher themselves, not a PR department. And honestly I think that's the right model — researchers are the best advocates for their own work, they just need platforms that let them speak directly to audiences without institutional gatekeeping. What I find really exciting is that social media collapses the distance between "promotion to peers" and "promotion to the public" — the same tweet can reach a cardiologist AND a curious person who just wants to understand how their heart works, and that dual reach is something no traditional dissemination channel has ever managed. The only real limitation I'd flag is that promotional success on these platforms does reward a certain kind of personality and time investment that not everyone can offer equally, which is worth acknowledging as a structural issue for how we think about visibility in academia.

Promotion is something I feel really strongly about because there's still this weird stigma in academia around "self-promotion" — like if you're actively pushing your work out into the world, you're somehow being immodest or unscholarly, which is honestly such an outdated attitude. If you've done good research, you have an OBLIGATION to make sure people know it exists! Twitter has been incredible for this — a well-crafted tweet about a new finding can generate more interest in 24 hours than a paper sitting in a journal for six months. And I don't just mean interest from other researchers; I mean journalists, policy people, educators, members of the public who might actually be affected by what you've found. That's the piece that excites me most. I've seen colleagues get media coverage and real-world uptake from research that would otherwise have been read by maybe 50 specialists, purely because they put the effort into communicating it accessibly on social media. The promotion angle also forces you to think about impact in a much more concrete way — who does this research matter to, and how do I reach them? I think it should honestly be part of every researcher's workflow, not treated as an optional extra you do if you happen to be a "social media person." We all need to be social media people now, whether we like it or not!
Same as above really, Twitter's been huge for getting work noticed OUTSIDE the usual academic bubble.

Similar to sharing -- Twitter has been incredible for getting work in front of people who actually CARE about it, not just other academics. I've seen posts about my research get picked up by science journalists and public interest accounts which honestly feels like the whole point of doing science communication in the first place!

Networking is honestly where I've had some of the most unexpected and exciting outcomes from social media — connections that would simply never have happened through conventional academic channels. Twitter in particular has this remarkable ability to collapse hierarchies that normally make it very difficult for a PhD student to get on the radar of established researchers: if you engage thoughtfully with someone's work publicly, they can see that and respond, and suddenly you're in a genuine intellectual exchange with someone whose papers you've been citing for years. That kind of lateral access is almost UNHEARD of in traditional academic networking, where geography and institutional prestige do so much of the filtering. I've made connections with researchers in exercise science, neuroscience, and nutrition — fields that touch my own work in physiology but that I'd have very little formal contact with otherwise — and a couple of those Twitter exchanges have evolved into real conversations about research directions and potential collaboration. It doesn't always lead somewhere, but the batting average is way higher than cold-emailing someone whose paper you admired. What I also find really valuable is that the networking isn't purely transactional — following researchers in adjacent fields and watching how they frame problems and methodological choices has shaped how I think about my own work in ways that are hard to quantify but feel genuinely significant. And honestly, running social media for a public science group has extended that network beyond academia altogether, connecting me with science communicators, journalists, and educators whose perspective on how research lands with a general audience is something I couldn't get from any SCN platform alone. That combination — peer networking AND public-facing networking through the same tools — is something I find really hard to replicate anywhere else

Networking is where I think social media has genuinely changed the landscape of academic collaboration in ways that would have been impossible even ten years ago. I've had direct conversations on Twitter with researchers at institutions I'd never have had any reason to contact otherwise — people working on questions that intersect with my own in ways I wouldn't have discovered through a literature search alone. There's something incredibly powerful about being able to just reach out to someone whose paper you found fascinating and have them respond within hours, as opposed to the old model of hoping you both happen to attend the same conference. For early career researchers and PhD students especially, that kind of access is HUGE — we don't have the established networks that senior academics have built over decades, so social media genuinely levels the playing field in a way I find exciting. I've also found that interdisciplinary collaborations are much more likely to emerge organically through social media than through formal channels, because you start following someone's work out of genuine curiosity and a conversation develops naturally from there. The serendipity of it is something I really value — you cant engineer that kind of connection in an email cold-call, but Twitter somehow makes it feel natural and mutual. It's not just about exchanging contact details at a conference anymore; it's about building real, ongoing intellectual relationships with people who genuinely care about the same questions you do, and for someone doing a PhD who doesn't yet have a big name or a full publication list, that visibility and accessibility honestly makes an enormous difference.
Huge. Found collaborators I'd NEVER have met through normal conference channels — Twitter especially just collapses the distance between researchers.

Networking has been one of the BEST unexpected benefits -- I've connected with researchers in completely different fields through Twitter just by following conversations about topics I find interesting. It's opened up collaborations I never would have found through formal channels alone.

I just want to say that filling out this survey has actually made me reflect on how much my professional identity has been shaped by social media in ways that feel almost impossible to separate out now — it's not a tool I USE for research, it's become part of how I THINK about research, how I communicate it, and why I do it. That probably sounds grandiose but I mean it genuinely.

The one thing I haven't had a chance to say anywhere in this survey is how frustrating it is that none of this engagement counts for anything in formal academic assessment. I spend real time and creative energy on science communication through Twitter and Facebook, I've built an audience of people who are genuinely interested in physiology, and that labour is essentially invisible when it comes to how a PhD student is evaluated or how a researcher is hired. That structural mismatch feels like a real problem — institutions SAY they value public engagement but the incentive architecture doesn't reflect that at all, and until it does, a lot of researchers who might otherwise lean into social media are going to keep treating it as a guilty pleasure rather than a legitimate part of their professional contribution.

If this survey shapes any policy thinking at Springer Nature I'd really love for that tension to be part of the conversation. The platforms exist, the public appetite exists — what's missing is institutional permission to take it seriously.

I just want to say that I think the academic community is at a genuine inflection point with social media, and I'm not sure everyone appreciates how much is at stake. The researchers who are still waiting on the sidelines, treating it as optional or slightly beneath them, are going to find themselves increasingly irrelevant to public discourse — not because the public doesn't care about their work, but because someone else will be there explaining it first, and not always accurately. That's actually what worries me MOST: the vacuum that disengaged researchers leave gets filled by people who may not have the expertise or the commitment to getting it right. Science communicators are doing incredible work but they cant be everywhere, and no one knows your research better than you do. So honestly my biggest takeaway from years of doing this alongside my PhD is that social media isn't a distraction from being a good researcher — it IS part of being a good researcher in 2017, full stop. I'd love to see that attitude shift institutionally, not just at the individual level. If universities and publishers and funding bodies started treating public engagement on social media as a legitimate measure of research impact rather than something you do in your spare time, I think you'd see a massive cultural change really quickly. The appetite is there on the public side — I see it every single day in the comments and shares and messages from people who are genuinely excited about science and just want someone to talk to them like an intelligent adult. We owe it to them, and honestly we owe it to ourselves, to show up and meet that appetite. I feel really lucky to have found that community early in my career and I hope this survey helps make the case for institutions to take it more seriously.

Keep doing what we're doing — social media is genuinely one of the most powerful tools scientists have for reaching people OUTSIDE the academic world and I dont think we're using it anywhere near its full potential yet.
Just that I think scientists have a genuine RESPONSIBILITY to be on these platforms -- the public appetite for science is there, we just need to meet them where they are!
